evidence_set: PET with [11C]DASB and arterial input in 13 people with a mean of 142 lifetime sessions, abstinent 2 to 8 weeks, against 13 matched comparison participants. Binding lower over all regions (F=27.07, p<0.001) and over cortical regions (F=25.65, p<0.001) but not subcortical (F=1.99, p=0.16); regionally significant in occipital (-0.01 vs 0.10, p=0.01), medial prefrontal (0.07 vs 0.13, p=0.04) and temporal cortex (0.07 vs 0.15, p=0.04), none surviving correction; caudate identical (0.77 in both groups) and putamen, thalamus, midbrain and hippocampus not significantly different (p=0.53 to 0.97). Editors' calculation (Hedges g, 95% interval centred on g): occipital -1.11 (-1.93 to -0.28), medial prefrontal -0.87 (-1.68 to -0.07), caudate 0.00 (-0.77 to 0.77). Binding values in six of the seven neocortical regions are near zero in both groups (the medial temporal lobe, 0.36 and 0.43, is the exception), so percentages from them are not interpretable.

Review of molecular imaging to November 2015 (one database, no appraisal of the studies): 16 human transporter studies, of which 14 found a significant reduction, with effect sizes from -0.05 to -2.17; of 10 studies measuring occipital cortex, 6 found their largest reduction there; 3 of 4 found significantly lower hippocampal binding (2 corrected for multiple comparisons); 11 reported lower thalamic binding but only 3 significantly. The review lists down-regulation or internalization, loss of neurones, lower protein expression and competition from released serotonin as explanations imaging cannot separate.

evidence_set: Review of molecular imaging to November 2015 (one database, no appraisal of the included studies): one animal and five human studies of the dopamine system, with no consistent effect in people. Of three dopamine transporter studies, one found striatal binding 13% higher than in polydrug controls (p=0.045, effect size 2.92) and 20% lower in users who had taken amphetamines within 3 weeks of the scan than in other MDMA users (p=0.007), which its authors read as an amphetamine effect, and two found no difference; dopamine D2/3 binding and release did not differ significantly in 9 people who had stopped (baseline binding 16 to 19% lower than in 8 polydrug controls, effect sizes -0.41 to -0.53); dopamine-synthesis capacity was 9% higher in the putamen than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, effect size 1.10) but no different from polydrug controls; a monkey study of the vesicular transporter found no significant difference.

evidence_set: PET with [11C]DASB and [11C]MDL 100907 in 13 people against 13: transporter binding lower over cortical regions (F=25.65, p<0.001) and unchanged subcortically, while 5-HT2A receptor binding was higher over cortical regions (F=14.55, p<0.001); across the seven cortical regions the size of the receptor increase went with the size of the transporter decrease at trend level only (r2=0.54, p=0.057, on percent differences in group means). No single regional comparison survived correction for multiple comparisons.

The review lists four explanations for lower binding that imaging cannot separate (down-regulation or internalization of the transporter, loss of the neurones expressing it, lower protein expression, and competition from released neurotransmitter), states that no PET or SPECT tracer directly assesses toxicity or degeneration, and notes that even if binding recovers it is unknown whether this means functionally intact neurones, citing a study in which people who had stopped for over a year had control-level binding but memory-test deficits similar to current users.

The review notes that human transporter studies have smaller effect sizes than animal studies (-0.05 to -2.17 against -0.38 to -20.03), that human exposure is estimated at 2-4 mg/kg for the one or two tablets typically taken (a person of 70 kg) against 20-141 mg/kg in the animal experiments, and that two studies suggest cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not account for the transporter findings. It records no pooled dose-response estimate.

evidence_set: In 13 people abstinent 2 to 8 weeks (mean 5.7), no correlation between length of abstinence and transporter or 5-HT2A binding reached significance; the authors note their narrow range of abstinence, and say the null result in 12 former users whose last use was over a year before the scan suggests the lower binding might be reversible, but urge caution before adopting that conclusion because that study had no group of people currently using and because cortical measurement with this tracer is noisy.
Results, 2nd (abstinence mean 5.7 weeks, range 2-8), 7th and 10th paragraphs; Discussion, 8th paragraph

The review summarizes the field as showing that transporter binding recovers after 40 to 200 days, without saying where the figures come from: the only 40-day figure in its text is a baboon study in which binding rose after the 40-day scan in pons, midbrain and hypothalamus but stayed low in cortex, and the 200 days matches the cross-sectional extrapolation for the pallidostriatum in a study that found no recovery in neocortex. It then asks whether recovered binding means functionally intact neurones, noting a study in which people who had stopped for over a year had control-level binding but memory-test deficits similar to current users, and concludes that the cause of any recovery is unknown.
